name: Sunk Cost Trap
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Money You Already Spent Should Never Decide What You Spend Next
lesson.summary: The sunk cost trap explains why past quantum spending, however large, is not a valid reason to keep funding a program, and why organizations fall for exactly this reasoning anyway.
lesson.body:
A sunk cost is money already spent that cannot be recovered no matter what you decide next. Classical decision theory is unambiguous here: sunk costs should play zero role in a forward-looking investment decision, only future costs and future benefits matter, because the past spending happens regardless of today's choice. Yet the sunk cost fallacy, letting past spending justify continued spending, is one of the most well-documented biases in organizational decision-making, largely because admitting a large past investment was wasted is personally and politically costly for whoever approved it.

Here is a worked example. A company has spent $40,000,000 over five years building an internal quantum computing team and a proprietary algorithm platform. A rigorous new analysis shows that finishing the remaining planned work will cost another $15,000,000 over two years, and even in the optimistic case, the completed platform will generate only $10,000,000 in value before it is likely superseded by newer technology. The forward-looking question is simple: is $15,000,000 in future cost justified by $10,000,000 in future benefit. Framed this way, the marginal ROI on the remaining spend is ($10,000,000 minus $15,000,000) divided by $15,000,000, which is negative 33.3 percent, a straightforwardly bad investment on its own terms.

The trap is in how the decision actually gets framed inside most organizations: as an all-up comparison of total losses rather than a forward-looking marginal one. "Walk away now with nothing to show for $40,000,000" feels different from "push forward and end up having spent $55,000,000 total for a platform worth $10,000,000," a $45,000,000 net loss either way once the full history is included. But the $40,000,000 is identical in both branches of the decision going forward, it mathematically cancels out, leaving only the real choice: spend $15,000,000 more to recover $10,000,000, a further $5,000,000 loss, or spend nothing more, a further $0 loss. Framed correctly, stopping is better by $5,000,000, and the fact that this feels harder to accept than the arithmetic suggests is the entire content of the bias.

This bias compounds inside large organizational quantum computing programs for structural reasons: the sums involved are large, the timelines are long enough that the people who approved the original spending are often still in charge when the continue-or-stop decision arrives years later, and the technology's ultimate payoff is genuinely uncertain enough that "a bit more funding might turn this around" is always superficially plausible, even when the numbers do not support it.

The fix is procedural, not just intellectual: build a fixed re-evaluation checkpoint into any multi-year quantum computing program from the start, an eighteen-month or three-year gate, where the only question asked is the forward-looking one from this book's own ROI framework, applied strictly to remaining costs and remaining benefits, with money already spent explicitly excluded from the memo. Organizations that install this gate in advance, before anyone knows which side of the decision they will be defending, make dramatically better capital allocation decisions than those that revisit sunk multi-year bets under the emotional and political pressure of the moment.
